  • Canvas: src/trigger_designer/qt/node_base.py, src/trigger_designer/qt/node_editor_colors.py
  • Theme hooks: src/trigger_designer/resources/qt/themes/base.qss, src/trigger_designer/qss/_style.scss
  • Icons: src/trigger_designer/qt/resources.json:98-105
  • Visual preview: docs/assets/design_system_preview.html in the source tree

items.title: Install Trigger Designer
items.text:
Alpha build

Trigger Designer 0.1.0a1 is an alpha release for Windows. It is a first public build: expect rough edges, and report what you find.

items.title: Download
items.text:
Go to the GitHub releases page and open the newest pre-release named v0.1.0-alpha.1. Download:

  • TriggerDesigner-0.1.0a1-windows-portable.zip (the program)
  • SHA256SUMS.txt (to check the download, see below)

The alpha has no installer. Unzip the archive anywhere you can write to, such as C:\Tools\TriggerDesigner, and keep the files together.

items.title: Check the download
items.text:
Open PowerShell in the folder with the files and run:

Get-FileHash .\TriggerDesigner-0.1.0a1-windows-portable.zip -Algorithm SHA256

The hash it prints must match the line for that file in SHA256SUMS.txt. If it does not match, download the file again.

items.title: First start: the Windows warning
items.text:
The alpha is not code-signed, so Windows may show a warning the first time you start it.

  1. Double-click TriggerEditor.exe.
  2. If the blue Windows protected your PC box appears, click More info.
  3. Click Run anyway.

Windows shows this warning for every unsigned program it has not seen before. It does not mean the file is known to be harmful. You can check the hash above first.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit

    The alpha ships as a 64-bit Windows build only. There is no Linux or macOS version.

  • About 500 MB free

    Space for the program itself. Your data needs its own space, on a drive you can write to.

  • Memory for the files you open

    Large files need more memory. See Limits and performance.

items.title: Where your data lives
items.text:
What Where Preferences and themes %APPDATA%\Trigger Designer Log files %APPDATA%\Trigger Designer\logs Run records (audit trail) Next to each workflow, in a <name>.runs folder

%APPDATA% is usually C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Roaming. Type %APPDATA% into the Explorer address bar to open it.

The program does not check for updates and does not send data anywhere. See Security and privacy.

items.title: Uninstall
items.text: Delete the program folder. To remove your settings too, delete %APPDATA%\Trigger Designer. Your workflow files and their run records stay where you saved them.

items.title: Known issues in alpha 1
items.text:
• Crash with code 0xC0000409. Under some heavy workloads (large files, many nodes running at once), the program can close without an error message. Windows records the crash as an application fault in Event Viewer. Save your work often and note the steps. This is the most important alpha risk.
  • Portable only. There is no installer and no Linux build in this alpha.
  • No update check. Watch the releases page for new versions.

Full release notes are on the GitHub release page.

items.title: Report a problem
items.text:
Open an issue with the Bug report template: new issue.

Give the version, the steps, and the file name of the log in %APPDATA%\Trigger Designer\logs. Do not attach workflow files or data files: they can hold business data. Describe the shape of the data instead.

For security problems, follow SECURITY.md.

items.title: Publishing the site
items.text:
The public site has two parts, served from one GitHub Pages deployment:

Path Source Built by / homepage/ nothing; plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript /docs/ docs/ Zensical, configured in zensical.toml

The two are separate on purpose. The landing page can change its look without touching the guide, and a page in docs/ can assume the reader already decided to install the app.

items.title: There is one live version
items.text:
The site is not versioned. Whatever is on main is what readers get. The alpha has no users who need to pin docs to an older release, and a version selector would double the surface to keep correct for every page.

Confirmed bug reports name the app version they came from, so an issue tells you which docs applied when it was filed.

items.title: How publishing works
items.text:
Publishing runs in CI, not from a workstation. .github/workflows/docs.yml runs on every push to main and on manual dispatch:

  1. it installs the docs dependency group;
  2. it builds docs/ into site/docs with Zensical;
  3. it copies homepage/ over the root of site/ and adds .nojekyll;
  4. it force-pushes site/ to the gh-pages branch.

The force-push means gh-pages is a build artifact, not a branch to commit to. Nothing is pushed from a local build.

items.title: Commands for a maintainer
items.text:
# Preview the documentation with live reload
uv run --group docs zensical serve

# Build exactly what CI builds, into site/docs
uv run --group docs zensical build --clean

# Preview the landing page on its own
python -m http.server 8000 --directory homepage

To check the assembled site the way it will be served, build the docs, copy the homepage over the root, and serve site/:

uv run --group docs zensical build --clean
cp -R homepage/. site/
python -m http.server 8000 --directory site

items.title: What gets published
items.text:
Everything in homepage/ and everything in docs/ except the paths listed under exclude_docs in zensical.toml. docs/internal/ holds engineering notes, plans and historical reports. It stays in the repository and never appears on the site.

Check a change before pushing: zensical build prints broken links and missing pages as warnings.

items.title: Blog
items.text:
Short how-to posts for Trigger Designer. Each post follows one task from start to finish on the portable build, 0.1.0a1.

  • Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV. Read a file, tidy the column names, and find duplicates.
  • Run a workflow and check the audit trail. Run it, verify the record, and export an HTML report.
  • Write a result to a file. Use File Output to save what a workflow produced.

The posts are written for the alpha. If a step does not match what you see, check Install and open an issue.

items.title: Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV
items.text:
This post builds one small workflow. It reads a CSV of orders, tidies the column names, and finds duplicate order numbers. It takes about ten minutes.

You need the portable build from the install page and any CSV with an order or invoice number column.
path: Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV

items.title: 1. Start a new workflow
items.text: Start Trigger Designer and click New Project. An empty canvas opens.
path: Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV

items.title: 2. Read the file
items.text:
Drag File Input from the Input tab onto the canvas. Select it, click the folder icon next to Source (tooltip Browse for file), and choose your CSV.

Open Window > Data Preview (Ctrl+Shift+D). The badge reads evaluated - not run. That means you are looking at the first 100 rows, which is a sample.
path: Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV

items.title: 3. Tidy the column names
items.text:
Press Shift+A on the empty canvas, type Norm, and press Enter. A Normalize node appears. Drag from the right socket of File Input to the left socket of Normalize. The default settings (trim spaces, spaces to underscores) are fine.

Click the empty canvas, then look at the preview. A column named Order ID is now Order_ID.
path: Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV

items.title: 4. Find the duplicates
items.text:
Add a Duplicates node from the Audit tab and connect Normalize to it. A red ! appears: the node needs a key column.

Select Duplicates. Under Match on, click None, then tick Order_ID. Leave Match type on Exact. Click the empty canvas to clear the red mark.
path: Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV

items.title: 5. Write the result
items.text:
Duplicates has three outputs. D holds the duplicate rows, U the unique rows, and S a one-row summary.

Add a File Output node and connect D to it. Set File to a full path, such as C:\Work\Orders\duplicates.csv. The format is CSV.

Nothing is written yet. File Output writes only when you run the workflow.
path: Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV

items.title: 6. Save and run
items.text:
Press Ctrl+S and save the workflow as orders_check.tds. Then click the play button (tooltip Run workflow).

Each node turns purple while it runs, then green. Open the Logs tab to see the run summary.
path: Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV

items.title: 7. Read the result
items.text:
Select Duplicates, then choose the S socket in the chip at the top of the Data Preview. The badge now reads from Run, and the summary gives the count of duplicate rows and groups.

Open duplicates.csv in the folder you chose. It holds the duplicate rows with two extra columns, dup_group_id and dup_count.
path: Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV

items.title: What to remember
items.text: The preview is a sample of 100 rows. Press Run before you quote a number. The next post shows how a run leaves a record you can verify.
path: Your first workflow: find duplicate rows in a CSV

items.title: Run a workflow and check its audit trail
items.text:
A Run processes all the data, not the sample. Each Run also leaves a record that you can check later. This post follows the record from the first Run to a comparison of two Runs.

You need a saved workflow that has finished one Run, such as the one from the first workflow post.
path: Run a workflow and check its audit trail

items.title: 1. Open Run History
items.text: Open Window > Run History. Run 1 is listed with the status ok.
path: Run a workflow and check its audit trail

items.title: 2. Verify the record
items.text: Click the Verify run log icon. The status line reports that the chain is verified, with a short code shown as the head of the chain. A verified chain means the record has not been changed since it was written.
path: Run a workflow and check its audit trail

items.title: 3. Read the summary
items.text:
Select the run and read the Summary pane. It shows:

  • a fingerprint of each input file, so you can tell whether the file changed;
  • the number of nodes that ran;
  • how row counts were taken.
path: Run a workflow and check its audit trail

items.title: 4. Export a report
items.text: Click Export selected run as HTML report and save the page. You can attach it to a workpaper or send it to a reviewer.
path: Run a workflow and check its audit trail

items.title: 5. Compare two runs
items.text:
Run the workflow again on the same, unchanged file. Run 2 appears in the list. Select both runs and press Compare two selected runs. With no changes, the comparison shows no differences.

Now change the duplicate key, run again, and compare. The comparison lists the setting that changed. That is the point of the record: you can show exactly what differs between two runs.
path: Run a workflow and check its audit trail

items.title: Where the record lives
items.text: Run records are saved in a <workflow name>.runs folder next to the workflow file. Keep that folder with the workflow if you share it. The record can be read, but changing it breaks the verification.
path: Run a workflow and check its audit trail

items.title: Write a result to a file
items.text:
Most workflows end by saving a result. This post shows the File Output node: the settings, the formats, and the one thing that stops people, which is that nothing is written until you run the workflow.

You need a workflow with at least one table to save, such as the output of Normalize from the first workflow post.
path: Write a result to a file

items.title: 1. Add File Output
items.text: Open the Input tab in the palette and drag File Output onto the canvas. Connect the table you want to save to its input socket.
path: Write a result to a file

items.title: 2. Choose a path and format
items.text:
Select File Output. In File, type a full path such as C:\Work\Orders\clean_orders.csv, or click Browse for save location. Choose the Format: CSV, Parquet, Excel, JSON or NDJSON.

Use a folder you can write to. If the file is open in Excel, the run stops with a message that names the file. Close it and run again.
path: Write a result to a file

items.title: 3. Run it
items.text: Click the play button (tooltip Run workflow). File Output writes when its node runs, and the Logs tab records the file that was written.
path: Write a result to a file

items.title: 4. Check the file
items.text: Open the file in the folder you chose. Its row count should match the preview after a Run, not the 100-row sample.
path: Write a result to a file

items.title: Common questions
items.text:
• Nothing appeared on disk. Did you press Run? Editing and previewing never write a file.
  • The file is replaced on the next Run. File Output writes the same path each time it runs. Copy the file first if you need the old version. (Workpaper Output has its own rule for an existing file, described in the workpapers guide.)

For the full settings, see the node reference.
path: Write a result to a file

items.title: Writing node pages
items.text: Every node in the palette has one page under docs/nodes/<family>/. A reader arrives from the node index or from a search, wants to know whether the node solves their problem, and needs the exact settings. They do not need to know how the node is built.

items.title: Who you are writing for
items.text:
An auditor or analyst building a pipeline in the app. They know their data and their question. They may not know what a socket is, and they will not read a paragraph that starts with an engine name.

Write in the second person. Name controls exactly as the Config Dock shows them. Use bold for a control or a panel name and code font for a message code, a column name or a file name.

items.title: What never appears on a node page
items.text:
• Class names, module paths, or any path under src/.
  • Engine names and internals: no mention of the data frame library, the SQL engine, lazy plans, plans, or how a node is evaluated.
  • Design notes, performance measurements, or refactoring plans. Those belong in docs/internal/.

If you need to explain behaviour, describe what the user sees: rows in a socket, a column that appears, a badge, a message.

items.title: The page template
items.text:
Each page uses these sections, in this order. Drop a section only when the node genuinely has nothing to say there.

  1. Title - the node name exactly as the palette shows it.
  2. Opening line - one sentence: what the node does, phrased as a task.
  3. Purpose - two or three sentences. What comes out, and what question it answers.
  4. When to use it - the case it fits, and the neighbouring node to use instead when it does not fit.
  5. Inputs and outputs - the sockets and their letters, and which rows or columns leave by each one. This is the section readers re-read, so be exact.
  6. Settings - a table with four columns: Control, What it does, Default, When to change it. One row per control, in dock order. Include the icon-only buttons by their tooltip name.
  7. Worked example - a small table in, a small table out, and one sentence saying what changed. Keep it to five rows or fewer.
  8. Edge cases and limits - empty input, missing columns, type surprises, caps, and anything that behaves differently in a preview.
  9. Messages you may see - the user-visible codes, what they mean in plain language, and the fix. A table with Code, Message, What to do.
  10. Tips - one or two sentences, only if they add something the sections above do not.
  11. Related nodes - two or three links, each with the reason to follow it.

End every page with a link back to the family index:

Back to the [Preparation node index](index.md).

items.title: Preview versus Run
items.text:
Every node page states the rule in its own words, in Edge cases and limits:

While you edit, the node works on the first 100 rows and shows at most 100 output rows. A Run uses every row. Trust the Run.

Do not paste the same paragraph into all 39 pages. Say what the 100-row sample means for this node: a Count can only say 100, a Pivot can miss a header, an audit test can miss a duplicate that sits on row 4,000.

items.title: Icons
items.text:
Node icons are copied into docs/assets/node_icons/<Family>/<Name>.svg. A page in docs/nodes/<family>/ refers to one like this:

![Duplicates](../../assets/node_icons/Audit/Duplicates.svg)

A family index page uses the same path because it sits in the same directory. Never link into src/: the built site cannot serve it.

items.title: Links
items.text:
• To another node in the same family: [Filter](filter.md).
  • To a node in another family: [Aggregate](../preparation/aggregate.md).
  • To the family index: [Preparation nodes](index.md).
  • To a guide page: [Running workflows](../../guide/running-workflows.md).
  • To a section on the same page: [Settings](#settings).

Use relative links only. An absolute path or a link starting with / breaks in the published site, because the documentation is served from /docs/.

items.title: Before you commit a page
items.text:
1. Open the node in the app and read every control in the Config Dock. The page must list all of them.
  2. Check each message code against the app, not against an older note.
  3. Run uv run --group docs zensical build --clean and fix what it reports.
  4. Read the page once as a user who has never opened the app. If a sentence needs the source code to make sense, rewrite it.

items.title: Trigger Designer user guide
items.text:
Trigger Designer is a desktop program for building data checks without writing code. You draw a workflow on a canvas: read a file, clean it, test it (for duplicates, gaps, Benford's law and similar audit tests), and write the result. Everything runs on your own computer, and every run leaves a verifiable record.

This guide is for auditors and analysts who use the program. It is task-oriented and avoids programming terms.

items.title: On this page
items.text:
• Where to find what
  • Conventions used in this guide
  • Your first workflow in 10 minutes
  • Where to go next

items.title: Where to find what
items.text:
• The canvas and nodes

    Learn the screen, add nodes, connect them, undo, arrange.

  • The Config Dock, Data Preview, Logs and Problems

    Change a node's settings, look at data, read the logs and the problem list.

  • Running workflows

    Understand the difference between the quick preview and a real Run.

  • Errors and problems

    Understand an error message, or look up a TD- code.

  • Run history and the audit trail

    See the evidence of what I ran, verify it, compare two runs.

  • Files and formats

    Know what a .tds file is, which files I can read and write, how paths are stored.

  • Preferences

    Change the theme, shortcuts, error and audit settings.

  • Security and privacy

    Know what the program does and does not guarantee, and how to open a workflow from someone else.

  • Limits and performance

    Know how big my data can be and how to keep things fast.

  • Troubleshooting, FAQ and glossary

    Fix a common problem, or look up a word.

  • Node reference

    Find out what a particular node does and how to set it up.

  • Command line

    Run a workflow unattended from the command line.

  • Workpapers

    Produce a formatted Excel workpaper.

items.title: Conventions used in this guide
items.text:
• Bold is a name you will see on the screen: a menu entry, a button label, a panel title.
  • A path of names joined with > is a menu: File > Open Recent means open the File menu, then Open Recent.
  • Code font is a key, a file name or a code you may see, such as Ctrl+S or TD-SCH-001.
  • Most buttons in the program are icons only. Hover over one to read its name.
  • "The sample" means the first 100 rows of each input, which the program uses while you edit. "A Run" means processing all the data.

items.title: Your first workflow in 10 minutes
items.text:
You will find duplicate order numbers in a retail orders file. The workflow is four steps:

File Input  ->  Normalize  ->  Duplicates  ->  File Output (x2)
 read the        tidy the        test for        write the duplicates
 CSV             column names    duplicates      and the summary

The sample file is savedfiles\Example_2_Retail_Ledger\data\orders.csv in the Trigger Designer folder: 40,800 orders with deliberately messy headers such as Order ID (with spaces). If you work from an installed copy without that folder, use any CSV of your own that has an order, invoice or document number column and set the column name accordingly.

items.title: 1. Start and make a new workflow
items.text:
1. Start Trigger Designer. The Welcome to Trigger Designer dialog opens.
  2. Click New Project. (Or close the dialog and choose File > New, Ctrl+N.)

An empty canvas opens as a tab, with the node palette across the top (tabs Input, Preparation, Join, Transform, Report, Audit), the Node Configuration panel on the left, and the Logs, Data Preview and Run History tabs at the bottom.

items.title: 2. Read the file
items.text:
1. In the palette, click the Input tab and drag File Input onto the canvas.
  2. With the node selected, the Node Configuration panel shows its settings. Click the folder icon next to Source (tooltip Browse for file) and choose orders.csv. You can also paste the path into the box.
  3. The node recomputes. Open Window > Data Preview (Ctrl+Shift+D). You see the first 100 rows. The badge reads evaluated - not run: this is the sample, not the whole file.

Look at the column names: the first one is Order ID with spaces. We will tidy that.

items.title: 3. Clean it
items.text:
1. Press Shift+A over the empty canvas. In the search box that opens, type Norm and press Enter. A Normalize node appears at the pointer. (You could also drag it from the Preparation tab.)
  2. Drag from the round socket on the right of File Input to the socket on the left of Normalize.
  3. Click Normalize. Its default settings (Trim spaces and Spaces to underscores) are what we want. Click the empty canvas to let it compute, then look at the Data Preview: the first column is now Order_ID.

items.title: 4. Test it
items.text:
1. Add a Duplicates node from the Audit tab (or Shift+A and type Dup). Connect Normalize to it.
  2. The node shows a red "!" and a tooltip "Choose the key column." (TD-AUDIT-001). That is the program asking you for the one thing it needs.
  3. Select Duplicates. In the Match on section click None, then tick only Order_ID. Leave Match type on Exact.
  4. Click the empty canvas. The red mark goes. In the Result section, press the refresh icon (Count exceptions now): the sample has no duplicates.

That is correct for the sample and misleading for the file. The planted duplicates are further down. Only a Run looks at everything.

items.title: 5. Write the result
items.text:
Duplicates has three outputs, marked D (the duplicate rows), U (the unique rows) and S (a one-row summary of the test).

  1. Add a File Output node (Input tab). Connect the D socket of Duplicates to it.
  2. Select it. In File type a full path such as C:\Work\Orders\duplicates.csv (or use the icon Browse for save location). The Format is CSV.
  3. Add a second File Output, connect the S socket to it, and give it the path C:\Work\Orders\summary.csv.

Nothing is written yet; File Output only writes when you Run.

items.title: 6. Save
items.text: Press Ctrl+S, choose a folder and name the workflow orders_check.tds. The tab title loses its asterisk.

items.title: 7. Run
items.text:
1. Click the play button at the top-left of the canvas (tooltip Run workflow). It turns into a stop button while the Run is in progress.
  2. Each node lights up purple, then green, as it finishes. For a file this size it takes a moment.
  3. Open the Logs tab: it ends with the summary of the Run and a line "Run log saved: ...".

items.title: 8. Look at the result
items.text:
1. Select Duplicates and look at the Data Preview (choose the S socket in the socket chip at the top). The badge now says from Run. The summary says it found duplicates: 1590 of 40800 rows are in 790 duplicate groups.
  2. Choose the D socket to see the duplicate rows. They also have two extra columns, dup_group_id and dup_count.
  3. Open duplicates.csv and summary.csv in the folder you chose. They hold the same rows. (duplicates.csv has 1,590 rows, summary.csv has 1.)

items.title: 9. Look at the evidence
items.text:
1. Open Window > Run History. Run 1 is listed, status ok.
  2. Click the Verify run log icon. The status line says "chain verified ... head xxxxxxxx".
  3. Select the run and read the Summary pane: the fingerprint of the input file, the number of nodes, the row-count mode.
  4. Click Export selected run as HTML report to save a page you can attach to a workpaper.

Run it again later on an unchanged file: run 2 appears, and selecting both runs then pressing Compare two selected runs shows no differences. Change the Duplicates key, run again, and the comparison lists the changed setting. See Run history and the audit trail.

items.title: If something goes wrong
items.text: Symptom What to do The Data Preview says "Select a node to preview its output" Click a node first. Normalize still shows Order ID Click the empty canvas to let the node recompute; check the connection from File Input. The Duplicates node keeps its red mark Make sure at least one column is ticked under Match on. The Run does not start Look for a loop or for another Run in progress. See Running workflows. An error names a file The file is probably open in Excel; close it and Run again. See Troubleshooting. You want to start over File > New, or close the tab and discard changes.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• Browse the node reference to see what else the palette offers.
  • Open one of the examples in savedfiles\ (for instance 1. in-select.tds, with its data in data\) to see finished workflows. The folder savedfiles\Example_2_Retail_Ledger\ holds a larger exercise with a step-by-step setup guide.
  • Read Security and privacy before opening workflows that someone else sent you.

items.title: The canvas and nodes
items.text:
The canvas is where you build a workflow. Each box on it is a node (one step: read a file, remove duplicates, write a result). Lines between nodes are edges (the data flowing from one step to the next).

Back to the guide index

items.title: On this page
items.text:
• Add a node
  • Connect nodes
  • Select, move, copy and delete
  • Labels and groups
  • Arrange, grid and snapping
  • Zoom and move around
  • Undo and redo
  • Reading the signs on a node
  • Menus and shortcuts
  • If something goes wrong

items.title: Add a node
items.text:
There are three ways. All three put the node where your pointer is, and snap it to the grid when snapping is on.

Way How Drag from the palette The palette is the strip of tabs at the top of the window. Click a tab, then drag a node icon onto the canvas. If you drop it on top of an existing edge, the node is inserted into that edge. Right-click the empty canvas A searchable menu opens. Type to filter by name, press Enter to take the first match, or open a category and click a node. Press Shift+A The same searchable menu opens at the pointer.

The palette tabs are named by what the nodes do:

Palette tab Nodes Input File Input, File Output, Workpaper Output Preparation Aggregate, Cleansing, Date Helper, Filter, Find and Replace, Formula, Multi-Field Formula, Normalize, Record ID, Rows, Select, Select Records, Sort, Split, Text to Columns, Unique Join Append, Fuzzy Match, Join, Reconcile, Union Transform Count, Pivot, Running Total, SQL Query, Transpose, Unpivot, Window Report Comment, Data Profile, Graph Audit Benford, Duplicates, Gaps, Risk Filters, Sample

The palette itself is the authority on what is installed. Workpaper Output is described in workpaper.md.

The right-click menu uses the same groups, except that the first one is called Input/Output. Every node has its own page in the node reference.

To hide or show the palette, use Window > Nodes Toolbar.

items.title: Connect nodes
items.text:
Drag from a round socket on one node to a socket on another. Outputs are on the right of a node, inputs on the left.

Rules the canvas enforces (a connection that breaks one simply does not attach):

  • An edge always runs from an output to an input. You may start the drag from either end.
  • You cannot connect two outputs together or two inputs together.
  • You cannot connect a node to itself.
  • You cannot create a loop. If the target already leads back to the source, the connection is refused.
  • An input accepts one edge. The exception is Union, whose single input accepts any number of edges.
  • An output can feed any number of inputs.

Some nodes have several outputs. Duplicates, for example, has three, labelled D (the duplicate rows), U (the unique rows) and S (a one-row summary). The letters beside the sockets tell them apart.

To change how an edge is drawn, right-click it and choose Bezier Edge, Direct Edge or Square Edge. This is only appearance.

To remove an edge, select it and press Del.

A workflow that already contains a loop (for example an older file) still opens, and the app tells you where the loop is. It cannot run until you remove one of the connections in it.

items.title: Select, move, copy and delete
items.text:
To Do this Select one node Click it. The Config Dock shows its settings. Select several Drag a rectangle on the empty canvas, or hold Ctrl or Shift and click nodes. The Config Dock stays empty when more than one node is selected. Move Drag a node. All selected nodes move together. Copy / Cut / Paste Edit > Copy (Ctrl+C), Edit > Cut (Ctrl+X), Edit > Paste (Ctrl+V). Copying keeps the connections between the copied nodes. Delete Edit > Delete or Del.

Paste works between workflow windows. Pasting something that is not node data (for example ordinary text) is ignored, and the status bar says so.

Copy a group header to copy the whole group with its nodes and the connections between them.

items.title: Labels and groups
items.text:
Labels are short notes that float above a node, for example "Customers 2024". They are saved with the workflow.

  • Click the text box above a node and type. Enter or clicking away keeps it, Esc cancels.
  • Or right-click a node and choose Set Label... (an empty label removes it).
  • A single node has a checkable Show Label entry. With several nodes selected you get Show Labels and Hide Labels.
  • The Config Dock also has a Label row at the top of every node's settings.

A label with no text is never shown.

Groups draw a coloured box around nodes that belong together (for example "Joins" or "Enriched").

To Do this Create a group Select two or more nodes, then press G, or choose Edit > Group selected, or right-click a node and choose Group Selected Nodes. Move a group Drag its title bar. The nodes inside move with it. Add a node Drag the node onto the group. Take a node out Right-click it and choose Detach from Group. Collapse or expand Press C, or use the + / - on the title bar. Edges that leave the group are drawn to the box while it is collapsed. Rename Double-click the title bar. Ungroup (keeps the nodes) U or Shift+G, or Edit > Ungroup. Delete group and nodes Select the group header and press Del.

The single-letter shortcuts are ignored while you are typing in a text box.

items.title: Arrange, grid and snapping
items.text:
Edit > Arrange tidies the selected nodes without moving them somewhere else (they keep the selection's top-left corner or centre). The same commands are in the right-click menu of a node, under Arrange. A command is greyed out until enough nodes are selected.

Command Needs Default shortcut Align Horizontal Centers 2 nodes Ctrl+Shift+H Align Vertical Centers 2 nodes Ctrl+Shift+V Distribute Horizontally 3 nodes none Distribute Vertically 3 nodes none Arrange in Row 2 nodes none Arrange in Column 2 nodes none Arrange in Grid 2 nodes none Snap Selection to Grid 2 nodes none Snap to Grid (a check mark, not a command) none none

You can change the shortcuts in Edit > Settings > Shortcuts (see Preferences).

Snap to Grid makes nodes land on the grid while you drag. Hold Alt while dragging to move a node freely. The setting is on by default and is also in Edit > Settings > Editor (grid size 10 to 100 px, default 20; show or hide the grid; snapping).

Any command that would change nothing does not add an undo step.

items.title: Zoom and move around
items.text:
Four round buttons float at the top-left of every workflow window.

Button (tooltip) What it does Run workflow / Cancel run See Running workflows. They share one place: only one is visible at a time. Zoom in Zoom in one step. Zoom out Zoom out one step. Fit view Zoom and centre so that every node is visible (it does nothing on an empty canvas).

Ctrl + mouse wheel also zooms. The plain wheel scrolls the canvas up and down, Shift + wheel scrolls it sideways, and dragging with the middle mouse button pans. The status bar shows the canvas coordinates under the pointer.

When you zoom far out, the canvas can draw simpler nodes to stay fast. You control this in Edit > Settings > Editor > Rendering (see Preferences). It affects drawing only, never your data.

F11 toggles full screen.

items.title: Undo and redo
items.text:
Edit > Undo (Ctrl+Z) and Edit > Redo (Ctrl+Shift+Z) work on a timeline of the last 200 steps per workflow. The menu names the step, for example "Undo Node label changed", so you can see what you are about to reverse.

What counts as one step:

Action Steps Creating, moving, connecting or deleting nodes One step each action. Changing a setting in the Config Dock (a checkbox, a drop-down, a chosen column) One step, named after the change. Typing in a text box A burst of typing is one step. Undo returns to what the box held before you started typing. Adding a rule, section or mapping row One step per click. Aligning, distributing or arranging One step per command. Setting a label on several nodes at once One step.

Things that are not on the timeline: selecting nodes, scrolling, zooming, and running the workflow. Opening a file starts a fresh timeline, so you cannot undo past the moment you opened it.

After an undo, the Config Dock refreshes to show the restored values for the node you have selected.

items.title: Reading the signs on a node
items.text: A node tells you its state in three places: a ring around its body, a round badge on its bottom edge, and a tooltip.

items.title: The ring
items.text:
Ring Meaning None The node is idle. Orange The node is selected (or under the pointer). Purple The node is running right now (during Run). Green The node finished during the last Run. It fades about a second after the whole Run succeeds. Red The node has a problem (it failed, or it cannot be computed). It stays until the problem is fixed.

Colours come from the active theme, so they may look slightly different in a light theme.

items.title: The badge on the bottom edge
items.text: Badge Meaning A small status icon The node's normal state: up to date, waiting to be recomputed, or invalid. Red "!" The node has an error. It replaces the normal status icon. Hover the node to read the message. Amber "!" A warning, or a node that was skipped. Amber "!" with the tooltip "Changes pending - the node runs when you click away" The yellow changes not run yet mark. See below.

items.title: "Changes not run yet" (the yellow mark)
items.text:
When you change a setting in the Config Dock, the new value is stored at once (and is saved and undoable), but most nodes do not recompute on every keystroke. Instead the node shows the yellow "!" until you leave it: select another node, click the empty canvas, or close the window. At that moment the node recomputes on the live sample and the mark disappears. Save and Run do not need you to leave the node first: they pick up the current settings themselves.

Data Profile and Comment are the exceptions: they update straight away.

items.title: The tooltip
items.text: Hover a node with a red or amber badge to read a short message: which node, what is wrong, the first sentence of the detail, a suggested fix, and the error code such as TD-SCH-001. The same problem is listed in the Logs dock. See Errors and problems.

items.title: Menus and shortcuts
items.text:
The menu bar sits in the title row of the window.

Menu Entries File New (Ctrl+N), Open (Ctrl+O), Open Recent, Save (Ctrl+S), Save As... (Ctrl+Shift+S), Exit (Ctrl+Q) Edit Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, Group selected, Ungroup, Collapse/Expand group, Arrange (submenu), Settings Window Nodes Toolbar, Show Logger, Data Preview (Ctrl+Shift+D), Problems, Run History, Node Configuration, Save Current Layout, Reset Layout, Close, Close All, Tile, Cascade, Next, Previous, and a list of the open workflows Help About

Other keys on the canvas:

Key Action Shift+A Open the add-node menu at the pointer G, U / Shift+G, C Group, ungroup, collapse or expand groups Del Delete the selection Ctrl+Shift+T Write the run statistics (runs, total and average time) to the Logs Ctrl+Shift+R Reset those statistics F11 Full screen

Workflows open as tabs in the middle of the window. Close a tab with its x; if it has unsaved changes the app asks whether to save, discard or cancel. If a save fails (for example the folder is read-only or the disk is full), a Save failed dialog shows the reason, the status bar says the changes are not saved, and the tab stays open with its unsaved changes.

items.title: If something goes wrong
items.text: Symptom What to do The edge snaps back when I drop it You broke a rule: output to input only, no loop, one edge per input (except Union). Try the other direction, or check for an existing edge on that input. A node has a red ring and a red "!" Hover it, or open the Logs dock. See Errors and problems. A node shows an amber "!" and nothing changed Click the empty canvas. The "changes not run yet" mark clears when the node recomputes. Paste does nothing The clipboard does not hold nodes copied from this app. The status bar says "Paste ignored: clipboard does not contain node data". The Config Dock is empty Select exactly one node. With none or several selected it stays empty. After undo, the dock seems unchanged Click the node again. The dock normally refreshes by itself; if it does not, tell your administrator. A box labelled Unknown appears The workflow uses a node this version does not have. Its settings are kept; see Files and formats.

items.title: The command line
items.text:
trigger-designer-cli runs a saved workflow with no window and nobody at the keyboard. It is meant for two situations: you want the same check to run every night or every month without opening the program, or IT wants to start a workflow from a script or a job scheduler and read a clear pass/fail answer.

It runs the same nodes as the editor, so a workflow gives the same result headless as it does when you press Run. It writes the same run record, and it adds protections that matter when nobody is watching: outputs are never left half-written, a workflow written by someone else will not run until you have approved it, and every outcome is a fixed exit code.

Back to the guide index

This page is both the guide and the command reference.
